extra.message: User input from params['id'] is concatenated directly into an SQL query string passed to cursor.execute(). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the 'id' parameter, e.g. /users?id=1 OR 1=1 to dump all users including session tokens.

User input from params.get('password')[0] is concatenated directly into an SQL query. While the username is sanitized with re.sub(r"[^\w]", ''), the password parameter has no sanitization. An attacker can bypass authentication with password=' OR '1'='1.

User input from params.get('msg') is returned directly as HTML content without any escaping or sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript via the 'msg' parameter, e.g. /post?msg=<script>alert(1)</script>.

Comment data retrieved from the database is rendered into HTML using str.format() without escaping. An attacker can store a malicious script via /guestbook?comment=<script>alert(1)</script>, which will execute when any user views the guestbook.

User data (username, firstname, lastname, email) from the database is rendered into HTML using str.format() without escaping on the profile page. An attacker who sets their email to <script>alert(1)</script> via the settings page can achieve stored XSS when the profile is viewed.

User data (firstname, lastname, email) from the database is placed directly into HTML input value attributes without escaping. An attacker can break out of the attribute with a payload like "><script>alert(1)</script> to achieve stored XSS.

User input from params.get('domain')[0] is concatenated into a shell command string and executed with subprocess.check_output(shell=True). An attacker can inject arbitrary OS commands via the 'domain' parameter, e.g. /diag?domain=www.google.com;whoami.

The HTTP BDR method handler passes self.path[1:] (the raw URL path minus the leading slash) directly to subprocess.check_output() with shell=True. An attacker sending a BDR request like 'BDR /whoami;id HTTP/1.1' can execute arbitrary OS commands with no authentication.

User input from params.get('object')[0] is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads(). An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary code upon deserialization, achieving remote code execution.

User input from params.get('path')[0] is passed to os.path.abspath() and then open(). The abspath() call does not prevent traversal; a path like ../../etc/passwd resolves to /etc/passwd and the file is opened and its contents returned to the attacker.
The StaticHandler.find() method uses the user-controlled request path directly in open('./{}'.format(path)). An attacker can request /../../../etc/passwd to read arbitrary files on the filesystem.

When the user-supplied path contains '://', urllib.request.urlopen() is called with the user-controlled URL. An attacker can make the server send requests to internal services, e.g. /docs?path=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ to access cloud metadata.

User input from params.get('path')[0] is injected into a JavaScript redirect via window.location.replace('{path}') without validation. An attacker can redirect users to malicious sites, e.g. /jump?path=https://evil.com. The path is also not JavaScript-escaped, enabling XSS via /jump?path=';alert(1);//.

User input from params.get('path')[0] is injected into JavaScript window.location = '{path}' without validation or escaping. This enables both open redirect and XSS attacks, e.g. /home?path=';alert(document.cookie);//.

The session ID is set directly from the URL parameter params.get('session')[0] via cookie['SESSIONID'] = session. An attacker can fix a victim's session by tricking them into visiting /home?session=ATTACKER_KNOWN_ID, then hijack the session after the victim authenticates.

The email change on /settings is performed via a GET request with no CSRF token. An attacker can craft a link like /settings?email=attacker@evil.com that changes the victim's email when visited, enabling account takeover.
Account deletion on /danger is performed via a GET request with no CSRF token. An attacker can craft a link like /danger?delete=1 that deletes the victim's account when visited.

The /admin page serves sensitive admin content (Manage Users, Update Database Settings links) before checking authentication. The redirect is only performed via client-side JavaScript, meaning the HTML body with admin links is fully delivered to unauthenticated users. A non-browser client can read the content.
Hardcoded credentials username='dsvpwa' and password='dsvpwa' are checked in the authentication logic. These cannot be changed without modifying the source code and provide a known login vector.
The SQL query on /users selects the 'session' column and renders session tokens in the HTML response (line 47). Any user accessing /users can see active session tokens, enabling session hijacking.

The response headers explicitly disable XSS protection (X-XSS-Protection: 0) and set a permissive Content-Security-Policy (default-src * 'unsafe-inline') that allows all resources and inline script execution, defeating CSP protections.

When SSL is enabled, the code explicitly re-enables SSLv3 (ctx.options &= ~ssl.OP_NO_SSLv3), re-enables compression (ctx.options &= ~ssl.OP_NO_COMPRESSION), and disables cipher server preference (ctx.options &= ~ssl.OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE). SSLv3 is vulnerable to POODLE, compression enables CRIME, and disabling cipher preference weakens the negotiation.

cwe: CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
